description.narrative:
Plateau State has experienced outbreaks of ethno-political violence since 1994. There has been repeated violent conflict in 2001, 2004, 2006, 2008, 2010 and 2011 leading to displacement of over 150,000 people, death of over 1000 people and destruction of property worth millions of pounds. The violence has tended to take the form of fighting between Christians and Muslims; however, despite their religious coloration the causes of the conflict are more complex and deep- rooted. Violence has often been the result of the long standing battle for control of political power and economic rivalry between different ethnic groups and between those labelled as “indigenes” and “non indigenes” or “settlers”.
The “indigenes” are considered the original inhabitants of the area, where as the “settlers” are newcomers to the state, although many have lived there for generations. Those considered as indigenes are Berom, Afizere, and Anaguta who are predominantly Christian by religion while Islam is the main religion among the Hausa-Fulani “settlers”. The widespread poverty and lack of education and employment in the state also play into the hands of politicians and leaders who wish to manipulate perceived injustices for their own benefit.
These conflicts which have been analyzed to be as a result of complex issues of political, socio-economic, ethnic and religious causes, have further widened the gap between the two major religious adherence and the various ethnic groups across the state. These crises have often led to untold hardship for women and children as well as the youths who form the bulk of the foot soldiers. The mental trauma and physical damage to houses and looting left a lot of communities in Jos seriously scarred by the experience. Many previously mixed neighborhoods; towns and villages are now either exclusively Christian or Muslim. The segregation of settlements according to religious lines has further heightened the suspicion and fear among the groups each suspecting the other side to be preparing to launch an attack.
The decision to establish a Dialogue and Peace Centre in Jos is to create a space where various religious and ethnic groups will use as a rallying point for organized dialogue fora for different stakeholders in peace building efforts.
